H1.text: A doctor checks your pulse three times. A tailor measures a sleeve twice. A cook tastes twice.

H2.text: Why measure the same thing again and again? Because no measurement is perfect.

H3.text: Diya pours one glass of water into a measuring jug, five times.

H4.text: Two forty eight. Two fifty two. Two fifty one. Two forty seven. Two fifty two millilitres.

H5.text: Same glass, five numbers. Which one is right? And how wrong is each?

P1.text: Every reading has a small error. The error is how far a reading is from the true value.

P2.text: We never know the true value exactly. Our best guess is the mean of all the readings.

P3.text: The five add up to twelve hundred and fifty. Divide by five. The mean is two hundred and fifty millilitres.

S1.text: Let's put the readings on our measuring bench.

S2.text: Each pour fills the jug to a slightly different mark. Watch the level.

S3.text: On the graph, each reading becomes a dot. The dashed line is the mean, two fifty.

S4.text: The gap between a dot and the mean is that reading's absolute error.

S5.text: Slow replay, reading one. Two forty eight minus two fifty is minus two. Its size is two.

S6.text: The other gaps are two, one, three and two. Some readings are above the mean, some below.

D1.text: Let's turn this into rules, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. The mean, a bar, is the sum of the readings, divided by n.

D3.text: Step two. The absolute error of each reading, delta a i, is the reading minus the mean.

D4.text: Step three. The mean absolute error is the average of the sizes of these errors. Here, ten divided by five. Two millilitres.

D5.text: Step four. So we write the result as two hundred and fifty, plus or minus two millilitres.

D6.text: The true value most likely lies between two forty eight and two fifty two.

R1.text: But is two millilitres a big error or a small one? It depends on what you measure.

R2.text: So compare the error with the value. Relative error equals the mean absolute error, divided by the mean.

R3.text: Two divided by two fifty is zero point zero zero eight.

R4.text: Multiply by one hundred, and you get the percentage error. Zero point eight percent.

T1.text: Remember this. Absolute error tells you how much. Relative error tells you how much compared to the value.

K1.text: Side by side. The glass: two hundred and fifty millilitres, error two. That is zero point eight percent.

K2.text: A spoon of cough syrup: ten millilitres, the same error of two. That is twenty percent.

K3.text: Now you try. Same absolute error. Which measurement is better? Pause and decide.

K4.text: The glass! Its error is a tiny part of the whole. For the syrup, the same two millilitres is a fifth of the dose.

V1.text: One more thing about the units.

V2.text: Absolute error has the same unit as the reading. Two millilitres.

V3.text: Relative error is millilitres divided by millilitres. The units cancel. It is a pure number.

V4.text: Your turn. Write the glass in litres instead. Does the percentage error change? Pause and decide.

V5.text: No! Two thousandths of a litre over a quarter litre is still zero point zero zero eight. Still zero point eight percent.

W1.text: Worked example. Diya times ten swings of a pendulum, five times.

W2.text: Nineteen point eight, twenty point two, twenty point one, nineteen point seven, twenty point two seconds.

W3.text: The sum is one hundred. So the mean is twenty point zero seconds.

W4.text: The error sizes add to one point zero. Their mean is zero point two seconds.

W5.text: Relative error, zero point two over twenty. That is zero point zero one.

W6.text: So the time is twenty point zero, plus or minus zero point two seconds. A one percent error.

X2.text: Many students average the errors with their signs. Minus two, plus two, plus one, minus three, plus two.

X3.text: That sum is always zero, because the mean sits in the middle! Drop the signs first. Take the size of each error, then average.

E1.text: Where is this asked? As short numericals. From a set of readings, find the mean, the mean absolute error, or the percentage error.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Five readings of a length, in centimetres. Find the percentage error. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is C. Zero point seven percent.

A2.text: The mean is four point zero zero. The error sizes add to zero point one four, so the mean absolute error is zero point zero two eight.

A3.text: Zero point zero two eight over four, times one hundred, is zero point seven percent. Zero percent is the signs trap.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why do we use the mean of many readings as the true value?

Y3.text: Two. Why is the average of the errors, with their signs, always zero?

Y4.text: Three. Same absolute error on a big and a small value. Which has the bigger percentage error?

N1.text: Next time: Aarav's study table has a small error in its length and its width. What is the error in its area? Error propagation.
